person.name: Contributor 01
person.overview:
Contributor 02 proposed Atlas to make fragmented equipment-return requests visible, retained policy and approval, and asked me to investigate the handoffs. This establishes the origin and mandate, not that I originated the trial.

The trial changed how I framed missed handoffs: instead of automatically chasing each one myself, I began asking whether ownership and escalation were clear enough for someone else to act, while still helping with exceptions. This is my attributed reflection, not a measure of team performance or proof of a career-wide trait.

accounts.title: Atlas / North Desk trial
accounts.summary:
Contributor 02 proposed Atlas to make fragmented equipment-return requests visible, retained policy and approval, and asked me to investigate the handoffs. This establishes the origin and mandate, not that I originated the trial.

By April the original North Desk team still used the form and escalation note; Contributor 04 and the coordinator handled review and exceptions, while the second-desk trial was later deferred for lack of supervised-shift staffing. This shows continued use only by the original team. Time saved and transferability remained unmeasured; deferral was a staffing constraint, not proof of failure.

This is my attributed reflection, not a measure of team performance or proof of a career-wide trait.
accounts.context:
Contributor 02 proposed Atlas to make fragmented equipment-return requests visible, retained policy and approval, and asked me to investigate the handoffs. This establishes the origin and mandate, not that I originated the trial.

The one-team trial split responsibility: I owned form implementation and defect follow-up; Contributor 02 owned policy, Contributor 03 checked wording, and Contributor 04 owned daily operations, ran the first shift, and kept the printed fallback available. Approval did not itself establish deployment; operational credit belongs to Contributor 04.
accounts.aim: I traced requests through three handoffs and chose to add next-owner and return-date fields to the existing shared form instead of a new application, because volunteers shared a computer and another login would add a step. The source supports this scoped design decision for a limited trial, not a broader product strategy.
accounts.contribution:
I implemented separate owner and approver fields, return-date validation, and a printed fallback list; Contributor 03 supplied the policy correction. The implementation record alone does not establish use.

Contributor 05 found a midnight date defect and supplied test cases; I investigated it, reproduced it, changed conversion to use the desk date, and tested both entry routes until they preserved the entered date. Contributor 05 owns discovery; my contribution was diagnosis, implementation, and testing of the correction.

The two exceptions showed me that a form could not resolve policy ambiguity, so I chose a visible escalation note over another status label, implemented it beside the approver field, and kept the printed fallback aligned; Contributor 03 reviewed the wording. Independent volunteer use of the note was not tested at delivery.
decisions: I traced requests through three handoffs and chose to add next-owner and return-date fields to the existing shared form instead of a new application, because volunteers shared a computer and another login would add a step. The source supports this scoped design decision for a limited trial, not a broader product strategy.

My first draft wrongly combined owner and approver. After Contributor 03 identified the policy boundary, I separated the fields and recorded that I should have checked it before drafting. I own the design mistake and correction; Contributor 03 owns the policy insight.
I offered to add return reminders only if the coordinator agreed who would respond, and I explicitly recorded that I had not built them. This was a conditional offer, not delivered work.
